entities.summary:
Durandus of Saint-Pourçain (1272–1334), a French Dominican friar, emerged as one of the most intellectually provocative figures of late medieval scholasticism, earning the epithet *Doctor Resolutissimus* for his bold, independent philosophical and theological critiques. Born in Saint-Pourçain-sur-Sioule, Auvergne, he rose through the ranks of the Dominican Order, becoming a Master of Theology at the University of Paris in 1312 and later serving as Bishop of Limoux (1317), Le Puy-en-Velay (1318), and Meaux (1326) under the Avignon Papacy. His significance lies in his systematic challenge to the burgeoning Thomistic synthesis of faith and reason, advocating for a more radical separation that anticipated later nominalist trends.

His primary contribution was his monumental *Commentary on the Sentences* of Peter Lombard, a work he revised multiple times, each iteration progressively departing from established Dominican doctrine, particularly that of Thomas Aquinas. Durandus questioned the real distinction between essence and existence, the nature of universals, the causality of the sacraments, and the divine concursus with created agents, often grounding his arguments in an empiricist epistemology that emphasized individual experience over abstract speculation. He rejected many of Aquinas's metaphysical proofs, arguing that certain truths, while demonstrable, were not necessarily evident to human reason alone, thereby asserting the primacy of divine revelation and the limitations of philosophical inquiry in theological matters.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Durandus of Saint-Pourçain's systematic critiques of Thomism and his advocacy for a more radical empiricism profoundly shaped late medieval scholasticism, influencing subsequent philosophical and theological discourse well into the Renaissance. His work contributed to the intellectual ferment that challenged established doctrines and paved the way for new modes of thought.
